source.stem:
Multiple choice questions.

System of equations

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 3 x + 4 y = 5, \\ - 7 x + 9 y = - \frac {5}{2} \end{array} \right.
$$

The solution is ( ).

(A) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l}x = 2,\\ y = -0.25 \end{array} \right.$

(B) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l}x = -5.5,\\ y = 4 \end{array} \right.$

(C) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l}x = 1,\\ y = 0.5 \end{array} \right.$

(D) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l}x = -1,\\ y = -0.5 \end{array} \right.$

hinge.title: Can I keep the direction of a divisibility claim straight when adding or subtracting numbers?

mx.name: condition_omission
mx.teacher_note: divisor still holds here even though The closure statement requires the same divisor to divide both starting numbers is missing from the stem — on the item about Can I keep the direction of a divisibility claim.

mx.name: relationship_reversal
mx.teacher_note: Multiple is what produces divisor, so the usual direction of this relation is run backwards — on the item about Can I keep the direction of a divisibility claim.

mx.name: scope_error
mx.teacher_note: The divisor rule also covers this: {'excluded_case': 'Do not use the closure rule unless the same divisor divides both starting numbers.', so it is not an exception — on the item about Can I keep the direction of a divisibility claim.

intelligence.enrichment: If a divides M and a divides N, then a divides M + N and M - N. The reverse direction is not forced: a total divisible by a can be split into addends that are not both multiples of a.
